title: Tuberculosis presenting as Anterior Mediastinal Mass: A Case Report
journal: JNMA: Journal of the Nepal Medical Association
case_prompt: A 20-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent evening fevers, headache, and vomiting, without cough, chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis, or weight loss. On examination, she was afebrile, and vital signs and systemic findings were normal. Neurologic examination showed neck stiffness; Kernig and Brudzinski signs were negative. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, white-cell count 7300 cells/µL (81% neutrophils, 15% lymphocytes, 1% monocytes, 0% eosinophils), and platelets 450 × 10^3/µL. Renal and hepatic function tests were normal, and HIV ELISA was negative. A chest radiograph showed soft-tissue enlargement along the right paratracheal stripe. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis supported tuberculous meningoencephalitis (Gram stain negative; adenosine deaminase 8 U/L). Brain MRI demonstrated ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema consistent with tuberculomas, and antitubercular therapy was initiated. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed an ill-defined, heterogeneously enhancing 4 × 4-cm mass in the anterior mediastinum, raising the possibility of a thymic lesion or confluent, necrotic lymph nodes.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Thymoma was considered as the mass arose in the anterior mediastinum and showed heterogeneous enhancement — “CECT scan of chest … revealed an ill-defined, heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the anterior mediastinum, suggestive of a thymic lesion…”  
2. Metastatic lymphadenopathy was considered because of necrotic-appearing nodes — “…suggestive of … confluent, necrotic lymph nodes (possibly tubercular or metastatic)…”  
3. Sarcoidosis was included in the differential of granulomatous masses but is typified by non-necrotizing granulomas — “Sarcoidosis is characterized by non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, while both tubercular and fungal granulomas may exhibit necrosis.”  
4. Fungal infection was considered among necrotizing granulomatous causes — “both tubercular and fungal granulomas may exhibit necrosis.”  
5. Tuberculosis was confirmed as the etiology on tissue examination — “The biopsy revealed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of tubercular origin.”
